entries.019053e8a0161757338d95140d30b9119b13c97b: <div sID="gen546" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Gen.15" sID="Gen.15"/> <div eID="gen546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen547" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen548" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have a solemn treaty between God and Abram concerning a covenant that was to be established between them. In the former chapter we had Abram in the field with kings; here we find him in the mount with God; and, though there he looked great, yet, methinks, here he looks much greater: that honour have the great men of the world, but "this honour have all the saints." The covenant to be settled between God and Abram was a covenant of promises; accordingly, here is, I. A general assurance of God's kindness and good-will to Abram, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. A particular declaration of the purposes of his love concerning him, in two things:—1. That he would give him a numerous issue, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.2-Gen.15.6">ver. 2-6</reference>. 2. That he would give him Canaan for an inheritance, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.7-Gen.15.21">ver. 7-21</reference>. Either an estate without an heir, or an heir without an estate, would have been but a half comfort to Abram. But God ensures both to him; and that which made these two, the promised seed and the promised land, comforts indeed to this great believer was that they were both typical of those two invaluable blessings, Christ and heaven; and so, we have reason to think, Abram eyed them.
entries.8d686be788b6c04a56805e60441dd17f6990370f: <div eID="gen548" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen547" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Covenant with Abram. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1913.)</title> <div sID="gen549" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After these things the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto Abram in a vision, saying, Fear not, Abram: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy shield, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy exceeding great reward. <div eID="gen549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen550" type="x-p"/> Observe here, I. The time when God made this treaty with Abram: <hi type="italic">After these things.</hi> 1. After that famous act of generous charity which Abram had done, in rescuing his friends and neighbours out of distress, and that, <hi type="italic">not for price nor reward.</hi> After this, God made him this gracious visit. Note, Those that show favour to men shall find favour with God. 2. After that victory which he had obtained over four kings. Lest Abram should be too much elevated and pleased with that, God comes to him, to tell him he had better things in store for him. Note, A believing converse with spiritual blessings is an excellent means to keep us from being too much taken up with temporal enjoyments. The gifts of common providence are not comparable to those of covenant love. <div eID="gen550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen551" type="x-p"/> II. The manner in which God conversed with Abram: <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord came unto Abram</hi> (that is, God manifested himself and his will to Abram) <hi type="italic">in a vision,</hi> which supposes Abram awake, and some visible appearances of the Shechinah, or some sensible token of the presence of the divine glory. Note, The methods of divine revelation are adapted to our state in a world of sense. <div eID="gen551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen552" type="x-p"/> III. The gracious assurance God gave him of his favour to him. <div eID="gen552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen553" type="x-p"/> 1. He called him by name—<hi type="italic">Abram,</hi> which was a great honour to him, and made his name great, and was also a great encouragement and assistance to his faith. Note, God's good word does us good when it is spoken by his Spirit to us in particular, and brought to our hearts. The word says, <hi type="italic">Ho, every one</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa. lv. 1</reference>), the Spirit says, <hi type="italic">Ho, such a one.</hi> <div eID="gen553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen554" type="x-p"/> 2. He cautioned him against being disquieted and confounded: <hi type="italic">Fear not, Abram.</hi> Abram might fear lest the four kings he had routed should rally again, and fall upon him to his ruin: "No," says God, "<hi type="italic">Fear not.</hi> Fear not their revenges, nor thy neighbour's envy; I will take care of thee." Note, (1.) Where there is great faith, yet there may be many fears, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2 Cor. vii. 5</reference>. (2.) God takes cognizance of his people's fears though ever so secret, and <hi type="italic">knows their souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.31.7">Ps. xxxi. 7</reference>. (3.) It is the will of God that his people should not give way to prevailing fears, whatever happens. Let the sinners in Sion be afraid, but fear not, Abram. <div eID="gen554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen555" type="x-p"/> 3. He assured him of safety and happiness, that he should for ever be, (1.) As safe as God himself could keep him: <hi type="italic">I am thy shield,</hi> or, somewhat more emphatically, <hi type="italic">I am a shield to thee,</hi> present with thee, actually caring for thee. See <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.24">1 Chron. xvii. 24</reference>. Not only the God of Israel, but a God to Israel. Note, The consideration of this, that God himself is, and will be, a shield to his people to secure them from all destructive evils, a shield ready to them and a shield round about them, should be sufficient to silence all their perplexing tormenting fears. (2.) As happy as God himself could make him: I will be <hi type="italic">thy exceedingly great reward;</hi> not only thy rewarder, but thy reward. Abram had generously refused the rewards which the king of Sodom offered him, and here God comes, and tells him he shall be no loser by it. Note, [1.] The rewards of believing obedience and self-denial are exceedingly great, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1 Cor. ii. 9</reference>. [2.] God himself is the chosen and promised felicity of holy souls—chosen in this world, promised in a better. He is the <hi type="italic">portion of their inheritance and their cup.</hi>
entries.fff423afc079761f05b3bd3d8f0b84175ac669b7: <div eID="gen555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen556" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> And Abram said, Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house <hi type="italic">is</hi> this Eliezer of Damascus? <hi type="super">3</hi> And Abram said, Behold, to me thou hast given no seed: and, lo, one born in my house is mine heir. <hi type="super">4</hi> And, behold, the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">came</hi> unto him, saying, This shall not be thine heir; but he that shall come forth out of thine own bowels shall be thine heir. <hi type="super">5</hi> And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he believed in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and he counted it to him for righteousness. <div eID="gen556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen557" type="x-p"/> We have here the assurance given to Abram of a numerous offspring which should descend from him, in which observe, <div eID="gen557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen558" type="x-p"/> I. Abram's repeated complaint, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.2-Gen.15.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. This was that which gave occasion to this promise. The great affliction that sat heavy upon Abram was the want of a child; and the complaint of this he here <hi type="italic">pours out before the Lord, and shows before him his trouble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.142.2">Ps. cxlii. 2</reference>. Note, Though we must never complain of God, yet we have leave to complain to him, and to be large and particular in the statement of our grievances; and it is some ease to a burdened spirit to open its case to a faithful and compassionate friend: such a friend God is, whose ear is always open. Now his complaint is four-fold:—1. That he had no child (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, to me thou hast given no seed;</hi> not only no son, but <hi type="italic">no seed;</hi> if he had had a daughter, from her the promised Messiah might have come, who was to be the seed of the woman; but he had neither son nor daughter. He seems to lay an emphasis on that, <hi type="italic">to me.</hi> His neighbours were full of children, his servants had children born in his house. "But <hi type="italic">to me,</hi>" he complains, "thou hast given none;" and yet God had told him he should be a favourite above all. Note, Those that are written childless must see God writing them so. Again, God often withholds those temporal comforts from his own children which he gives plentifully to others that are strangers to him. 2. That he was never likely to have any, intimated in that <hi type="italic">I go,</hi> or "<hi type="italic">I am going, childless,</hi> going into years, going down the hill apace; nay, I am going out of the world, going the way of all the earth. <hi type="italic">I die childless,</hi>" so the LXX. "I leave the world, and leave no child behind me." 3. That his servants were for the present and were likely to be to him instead of sons. While he lived, <hi type="italic">the steward of his house was Eliezer of Damascus;</hi> to him he committed the care of his family and estate, who might be faithful, but only as a servant, not as a son. When he died, <hi type="italic">one born in his house would be his heir,</hi> and would bear rule over all that for which he had laboured, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.18-Eccl.2.19">Eccl. ii. 18, 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.21">21</reference>. God had already told him that he would make of him <hi type="italic">a great nation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.2">ch. xii. 2</reference>), and his <hi type="italic">seed as the dust of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.16">ch. xiii. 16</reference>); but he had left him in doubt whether it should be his seed begotten or his seed adopted, by a son of his loins or only a son of his house. "Now, Lord," says Abram, "if it be only an adopted son, it must be one of my servants, which will reflect disgrace upon the promised seed, that is to descend from him." Note, While promised mercies are delayed our unbelief and impatience are apt to conclude them denied. 4. That the want of a son was so great a trouble to him that it took away the comfort of all his enjoyments: "<hi type="italic">Lord, what wilt thou give me?</hi> All is nothing to me, if I have not a son." Now, (1.) If we suppose that Abram looked no further than a temporal comfort, this complaint was culpable. God had, by his providence, given him some good things, and more by his promise; and yet Abram makes no account of them, because he has not a son. It did very ill become the father of the faithful to say, <hi type="italic">What wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless,</hi> immediately after God had said, <hi type="italic">I am thy shield, and thy exceedingly great reward.</hi> Note, Those do not rightly value the advantages of their covenant-relation to God and interest in him who do not think them sufficient to balance the want of any creature-comfort whatever. But, (2.) If we suppose that Abram, herein, had a eye to the promised seed, the importunity of his desire was very commendable: all was nothing to him, if he had not the earnest of that great blessing, and an assurance of his relation to the Messiah, of which God had already encouraged him to maintain the expectation. He has wealth, and victory, and honour; but, while he is kept in the dark about the main matter, it is all nothing to him. Note, Till we have some comfortable evidence of our interest in Christ and the new covenant, we should not rest satisfied with any thing else. "This, and the other, I have; but what will all this avail me, if I go Christless?" Yet thus far the complaint was culpable, that there was some diffidence of the promise at the bottom of it, and a weariness of waiting God's time. Note, True believers sometimes find it hard to reconcile God's promises and his providences, when they seem to disagree. <div eID="gen558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen559" type="x-p"/> II. God's gracious answer to this complaint. To the first part of the complaint (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.2">v. 2</reference>) God gave no immediate answer, because there was something of fretfulness in it; but, when he renews his address somewhat more calmly (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.3">v. 3</reference>), God answered him graciously. Note, If we continue instant in prayer, and yet pray with a humble submission to the divine will, we shall not seek in vain. 1. God gave him an express promise of a son, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.4">v. 4</reference>. This that is born in thy house <hi type="italic">shall not be thy heir,</hi> as thou fearest, but one that shall <hi type="italic">come forth out of thy own bowels shall be thy heir.</hi> Note, (1.) God makes heirs; he says, "This shall not, and this shall;" and whatever men devise and design, in settling their estates, God's counsel shall stand. (2.) God is often better to us than our own fears, and gives the mercy we had long despaired of. 2. To affect him the more with this promise, he took him out, and showed him the stars (this vision being early in the morning, before day), and then tells him, <hi type="italic">So shall thy seed be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">v. 5</reference>. (1.) So numerous; the stars seem innumerable to a common eye: Abram feared he should have no child at all, but God assured him that the descendants from his loins should be so many as not to be numbered. (2.) So illustrious, resembling the stars in splendour; for to <hi type="italic">them pertained the glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>. Abram's seed, according to his flesh, were like the dust of the earth (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.16">ch. xiii. 16</reference>), but his spiritual seed are like the stars of heaven, not only numerous, but glorious, and very precious. <div eID="gen559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen560" type="x-p"/> III. Abram's firm belief of the promise God now made him, and God's favourable acceptance of his faith, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">v. 6</reference>. 1. He <hi type="italic">believed in the Lord,</hi> that is, he believed the truth of that promise which God had now made him, resting upon the irresistible power and the inviolable faithfulness of him that made it. <hi type="italic">Hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?</hi> Note, Those who would have the comfort of the promises must mix faith with the promises. See how the apostle magnifies this faith of Abram, and makes it a standing example, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.19-Rom.4.21">Rom. iv. 19-21</reference>. <hi type="italic">He was not weak in faith; he staggered not at the promise;</hi> he was <hi type="italic">strong in faith; he was fully persuaded.</hi> The Lord work such a faith in every one of us! Some think that his believing in the Lord respected, not only the Lord promising, but the Lord promised, the Lord Jesus, the Mediator of the new covenant. He <hi type="italic">believed in him,</hi> that is, received and embraced the divine revelation concerning him, and <hi type="italic">rejoiced to see his day,</hi> though at so great a distance, <reference osisRef="John.8.56">John viii. 56</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">God counted it to him for righteousness;</hi> that is, upon the score of this he was accepted of God, and, as the rest of the patriarchs, by faith he <hi type="italic">obtained witness that he was righteous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.4">Heb. xi. 4</reference>. This is urged in the New Testament to prove that we are justified by faith without the works of the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.4">Rom. iv. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.6">Gal. iii. 6</reference>); for Abram was so justified while he was yet uncircumcised. If Abram, that was so rich in good works, was not justified by them, but by his faith, much less can we, that are so poor in them. This faith, which was imputed to Abram for righteousness, had lately struggled with unbelief (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.2">v. 2</reference>), and, coming off a conqueror, it was thus crowned, thus honoured. Note, A fiducial practical acceptance of, and dependence upon, God's promise of grace and glory, in and through Christ, is that which, according to the tenour of the new covenant, gives us a right to all the blessings contained in that promise. All believers are justified as Abram was, and it was his faith that was <hi type="italic">counted to him for righteousness.</hi>
entries.68ea0fcea7c651f4355dc795fe7f8d2186d145b1: <div eID="gen560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen561" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And he said unto him, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he said, Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it? <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said unto him, Take me an heifer of three years old, and a she goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon. 10 And he took unto him all these, and divided them in the midst, and laid each piece one against another: but the birds divided he not. <hi type="super">11</hi> And when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away. <div eID="gen561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen562" type="x-p"/> We have here the assurance given to Abram of the land of Canaan for an inheritance. <div eID="gen562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen563" type="x-p"/> I. God declares his purpose concerning it, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.7">v. 7</reference>. Observe here, Abram made no complaint in this matter, as he had done for the want of a child. Note, Those that are sure of an interest in the promised seed will see no reason to doubt of a title to the promised land. If Christ is ours, heaven is ours. Observe again, When he believed the former promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">v. 6</reference>) then God explained and ratified this to him. Note, To him that has (improves what he has) more shall be given. Three things God here reminds Abram of, for his encouragement concerning the promise of this good land:— <div eID="gen563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen564" type="x-p"/> 1. What God is in himself: <hi type="italic">I am the Lord</hi> Jehovah; and therefore, (1.) "I may give it to thee, for I am sovereign Lord of all, and have a right to dispose of the whole earth." (2.) "I can give it to thee, whatever opposition may be made, though by the sons of Anak." God never promises more than he is able to perform, as men often do. (3.) "I will make good my promise to thee." Jehovah is <hi type="italic">not a man that he should lie.</hi> <div eID="gen564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen565" type="x-p"/> 2. What he had done for Abram. He had brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, <hi type="italic">out of the fire of the Chaldees,</hi> so some, that is, either from their idolatries (for the Chaldeans worshipped the fire), or from their persecutions. The Jewish writers have a tradition that Abram was cast into a fiery furnace for refusing to worship idols, and was miraculously delivered. It is rather a place of that name. Thence God brought him by an effectual call, brought him with a gracious violence, snatched him as a brand out of the burning. This was, (1.) A special mercy: "I brought thee, and left others, thousands, to perish there." <hi type="italic">God called him alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.2">Isa. li. 2</reference>. (2.) A spiritual mercy, a mercy to his soul, a deliverance from sin and its fatal consequences. If God save our souls, we shall want nothing that is good for us. (3.) A fresh mercy, lately bestowed, and therefore should be the more affecting, as that in the preface to the commandments, <hi type="italic">I am the Lord that brought thee out of Egypt</hi> lately. (4.) A foundation mercy, the beginning of mercy, peculiar mercy to Abram, and therefore a pledge and earnest of further mercy, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.9">Isa. lxvi. 9</reference>. Observe how God speaks of it as that which he gloried in: <hi type="italic">I am the Lord that brought thee out.</hi> He glories in it as an act both of power and grace; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.29.22">Isa. xxix. 22</reference>, where he glories in it, long afterwards. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord who redeemed</hi> Abraham, redeemed him from sin. <div eID="gen565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen566" type="x-p"/> 3. What he intended to do yet further for him: "<hi type="italic">I brought thee</hi> hither, on purpose <hi type="italic">to give thee this land to inherit it,</hi> not only to possess it, but to possess it as an inheritance, which is the sweetest and surest title." Note, (1.) The providence of God has secret but gracious designs in all its various dispensations towards good people; we cannot conceive the projects of Providence, till the event shows them in all their mercy and glory. (2.) The great thing God designs in all his dealings with his people is to bring them safely to heaven. They are <hi type="italic">chosen to salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2 Thess. ii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">called to the kingdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.12">1 Thess. ii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">begotten to the inheritance</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3-1Pet.1.4">1 Pet. i. 3, 4</reference>), and by all <hi type="italic">made meet</hi> for it, <reference osisRef="Col.1.12-Col.1.13">Col. i. 12, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2 Cor. iv. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen567" type="x-p"/> II. Abram desires a sign: <hi type="italic">Whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">v. 8</reference>. This did not proceed from distrust of God's power or promise, as that of Zacharias; but he desired this, 1. For the strengthening and confirming of his own faith; he believed (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">v. 6</reference>), but here he prays, <hi type="italic">Lord, help me</hi> against <hi type="italic">my unbelief. Now</hi> he believed, but he desired a sign to be treasured up against an hour of temptation, not knowing how his faith might, by some event or other, be shocked and tried. Note, We all need, and should desire, helps from heaven for the confirming of our faith, and should improve sacraments, which are instituted signs, for that purpose. See <reference osisRef="Judg.6.36-Judg.6.40">Judg. vi. 36-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.8-2Kgs.20.10">2 Kings xx. 8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.11-Isa.7.12">Isa. vii. 11, 12</reference>. 2. For the ratifying of the promise to his posterity, that they also might be brought to believe it. Note, Those that are satisfied themselves should desire that others also may be satisfied of the truth of God's promises. John sent his disciples to Christ, not so much for his own satisfaction as for theirs, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.2-Matt.11.3">Matt. xi. 2, 3</reference>. Canaan was a type of heaven. Note, It is a very desirable thing to know that we shall inherit the heavenly Canaan, that is, to be confirmed in our belief of the truth of that happiness, and to have the evidences of our title to it more and more cleared up to us. <div eID="gen567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen568" type="x-p"/> III. God directs Abram to make preparations for a sacrifice, intending by that to give him a sign, and Abram makes preparation accordingly (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.9-Gen.15.11">v. 9-11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Take me a heifer,</hi> &c. Perhaps Abram expected some extraordinary sign from heaven; but God gives him a sign upon a sacrifice. Note, Those that would receive the assurances of God's favour, and would have their faith confirmed, must attend instituted ordinances, and expect to meet with God in them. Observe, 1. God appointed that each of the beasts used for this service should be three years old, because then they were at their full growth and strength: God must be served with the best we have, for he is the best. 2. We do not read that God gave Abram particular directions how to manage these beasts and fowls, knowing that he was so well versed in the law and custom of sacrifices that he needed not any particular directions; or perhaps instructions were given him, which he carefully observed, thought they are not recorded: at least it was intimated to him that they must be prepared for the solemnity of ratifying a covenant; and he well knew the manner of preparing them. 3. Abram took as God appointed him, though as yet he knew not how these things should become a sign to him. This was not the first instance of Abram's implicit obedience. He divided the beasts in the midst, according to the ceremony used in confirming covenants, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18-Jer.34.19">Jer. xxxiv. 18, 19</reference>, where it is said, They cut <hi type="italic">the calf in twain, and passed between the parts.</hi> 4. Abram, having prepared according to God's appointment, now set himself to wait for the sign God might give him by these, like the prophet upon his watch-tower, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab. ii. 1</reference>. While God's appearing to own his sacrifice was deferred, Abram continued waiting, and his expectations were raised by the delay; when <hi type="italic">the fowls came down upon the carcases</hi> to prey upon them, as common and neglected things, <hi type="italic">Abram drove them away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.11">v. 11</reference>), believing that the vision would, at the end, <hi type="italic">speak, and not lie.</hi> Note, A very watchful eye must be kept upon our spiritual sacrifices, that nothing be suffered to prey upon them and render them unfit for God's acceptance. When vain thoughts, like these fowls, come down upon our sacrifices, we must drive them away, and not suffer them to lodge within us, but <hi type="italic">attend on God without distraction.</hi>
entries.f31cab4f7cb1222f38e00093b27c5f5212a41985: <div eID="gen568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen569" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he said unto Abram, Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land <hi type="italic">that is</hi> not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years; 14 And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance. 15 And thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age. <hi type="super">16</hi> But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites <hi type="italic">is</hi> not yet full. <div eID="gen569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen570" type="x-p"/> We have here a full and particular discovery made to Abram of God's purposes concerning his seed. Observe, <div eID="gen570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen571" type="x-p"/> I. The time when God came to him with this discovery: <hi type="italic">When the sun was going down,</hi> or <hi type="italic">declining,</hi> about the time of the <hi type="italic">evening oblation,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.36">1 Kings xviii. 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan. ix. 21</reference>. Early in the morning, before day, while the stars were yet to be seen, God had given him orders concerning the sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">v. 5</reference>), and we may suppose it was, at least, his morning's work to prepare them and set them in order; when he had done this, he abode by them, praying and waiting till towards evening. Note, God often keeps his people long in expectation of the comforts he designs them, for the confirmation of their faith; but though the answers of prayer, and the performance of promises, come slowly, yet they come surely. <hi type="italic">At evening time it shall be light.</hi> <div eID="gen571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen572" type="x-p"/> II. The preparatives for this discovery. 1. <hi type="italic">A deep sleep fell upon Abram,</hi> not a common sleep through weariness or carelessness, but a divine ecstasy, like that which the <hi type="italic">Lord God caused to fall upon Adam</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.21">ch. ii. 21</reference>), that, being hereby wholly taken off from the view of things sensible, he might be wholly taken up with the contemplation of things spiritual. The doors of the body were locked up, that the soul might be private and retired, and might act the more freely and like itself. 2. With this sleep, <hi type="italic">a horror of great darkness fell upon him.</hi> How sudden a change! But just before we had him solacing himself in the comforts of God's covenant, and in communion with him; and here a <hi type="italic">horror of great darkness</hi> falls upon him. Note, The children of light do not always walk in the light, but sometimes clouds and darkness are round about them. This great darkness, which brought horror with it, was designed, (1.) To strike an awe upon the spirit of Abram, and to possess him with a holy reverence, that the familiarity to which God was pleased to admit him might not breed contempt. Note, Holy fear prepares the soul for holy joy; the spirit of bondage makes way for the spirit of adoption. God wounds first, and then heals; humbles first, and then lifts up, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.5-Isa.6.6">Isa. vi. 5, 6</reference>, &c. (2.) To be a specimen of the methods of God's dealings with his seed. They must first be in the horror and darkness of Egyptian slavery, and then enter with joy into the good land; and therefore he must have the foretaste of their sufferings, before he had the foresight of their happiness. (3.) To be an indication of the nature of that covenant of peculiarity which God was now about to make with Abram. The Old-Testament dispensation, which was founded on that covenant, was a dispensation, [1.] Of darkness and obscurity, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13-2Cor.3.14">2 Cor. iii. 13, 14</reference>. [2.] Of dread and horror, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">Heb. xii. 18</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen573" type="x-p"/> III. The prediction itself. Several things are here foretold. <div eID="gen573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen574" type="x-p"/> 1. The suffering state of Abram's seed for a long time, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.13">v. 13</reference>. Let not Abram flatter himself with the hopes of nothing but honour and prosperity in his family; no, he must know, of a surety, that which he was loth to believe, that the promised seed should be a persecuted seed. Note, God sends the worst first; we must first suffer, and then reign. He also lets us know the worst before it comes, that when it comes it may not be a surprise to us, <reference osisRef="John.16.4">John xvi. 4</reference>. Now we have here, <div eID="gen574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen575" type="x-p"/> (1.) The particulars of their sufferings. [1.] They shall be strangers; so they were, first in Canaan (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.12">Ps. cv. 12</reference>) and afterwards in Egypt; before they were lords of their own land they were strangers in a strange land. The inconveniences of an unsettled state make a happy settlement the more welcome. Thus the heirs of heaven are first strangers on earth, a land that is not theirs. [2.] They shall be servants; so they were to the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Exod.1.13">Exod. i. 13</reference>. See how that which was the doom of the Canaanites (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">ch. ix. 25</reference>), proves the distress of Abram's seed: they are made to serve, but with this difference, the Canaanites serve under a curse, the Hebrews under a blessing; and the <hi type="italic">upright shall have dominion in the morning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>. [3.] They shall be suffers. Those whom they serve shall afflict them; see <reference osisRef="Exod.1.11">Exod. i. 11</reference>. Note, Those that are blessed and beloved of God are often sorely afflicted by wicked men; and God foresees it, and takes cognizance of it. <div eID="gen575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen576" type="x-p"/> (2.) The continuance of their sufferings—<hi type="italic">four hundred years.</hi> This persecution began with mocking, when Ishmael, the son of an Egyptian, persecuted Isaac, who was <hi type="italic">born after the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.21.9">ch. xxi. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.29">Gal. iv. 29</reference>. It continued in loathing; for it was an abomination to the Egyptians to eat bread with the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Gen.43.32">ch. xliii. 32</reference>; and it came at last to murder, the basest of murders, that of their new-born children; so that, more or less, it continued 400 years, though, in extremity, not so many. This was a long time, but a limited time. <div eID="gen576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen577" type="x-p"/> 2. The judgment of the enemies of Abram's seed: <hi type="italic">That nation whom they shall serve,</hi> even the Egyptians, <hi type="italic">will I judge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.15.14">v. 14</reference>. This points at the plagues of Egypt, by which God not only constrained the Egyptians to release Israel, but punished them for all the hardships they had put upon them. Note, (1.) Though God may suffer persecutors and oppressors to trample upon his people a great while, yet he will certainly reckon with them at last; for his <hi type="italic">day is coming,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12-Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 12, 13</reference>. (2.) The punishing of persecutors is the judging of them: it is a righteous thing with God, and a particular act of justice, to recompense tribulations to those that trouble his people. The judging of the church's enemies is God's work: <hi type="italic">I will judge.</hi> God can do it, for he is the Lord; he will do it, for he is his people's God, and he has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine, I will repay.</hi> To him therefore we must leave it, to be done in his way and time. <div eID="gen577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen578" type="x-p"/> 3. The deliverance of Abram's seed out of Egypt. That great event is here foretold: <hi type="italic">Afterwards shall they come out with great substance.</hi> It is here promised, (1.) That they should be enlarged: <hi type="italic">Afterwards they shall come out;</hi> that is, either after they have been afflicted 400 years, when the days of their servitude are fulfilled, or after the Egyptians are judged and plagued, then they may expect deliverance. Note, The destruction of oppressors is the redemption of the oppressed; they will not let God's people go till they are forced to it. (2.) That they should be enriched: <hi type="italic">They shall come out with great substance;</hi> this was fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.35-Exod.12.36">Exod. xii. 35, 36</reference>. God took care they should have, not only a good land to go to, but a good stock to carry with them. <div eID="gen578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen579" type="x-p"/> 4. Their happy settlement in Canaan, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">v. 16</reference>. They shall not only come out of Egypt, but <hi type="italic">they shall come hither again,</hi> hither to the land of Canaan, wherein thou now art. The discontinuance of their possession shall be no defeasance of their right: we must not reckon those comforts lost for ever that are intermitted for a time. The reason why they must not have the land of promise in possession till the fourth generation was because <hi type="italic">the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full.</hi> Israel cannot be possessed of Canaan till the Amorites be dispossessed; and they are not yet ripe for ruin. The righteous God has determined that they shall not be cut off till they have persisted in sin so long, and arrived at such a pitch of wickedness, that there may appear some equitable proportion between their sin and their ruin; and therefore, till it come to that, the seed of Abram must be kept out of possession. Note, (1.) The measure of sin fills gradually. Those that continue impenitent in wicked ways are treasuring up unto themselves wrath. (2.) Some people's measure of sin fills slowly. The Sodomites, who were sinners before the Lord exceedingly, soon filled their measure; so did the Jews, who were, in profession, near to God. But the iniquity of the Amorites was long in the filling up. (3.) That this is the reason of the prosperity of wicked people; the measure of their sins is not yet full. The wicked <hi type="italic">live, become old, and are mighty in power,</hi> while God is <hi type="italic">laying up their iniquity for their children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">Matt. xxiii. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.34">Deut. xxxii. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen580" type="x-p"/> 5. Abram's peaceful quiet death and burial, before these things should come to pass, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.15">v. 15</reference>. As he should not live to see that good land in the possession of his family, but must die, as he lived, a stranger in it, so, to balance this, he should not live to see the troubles that should come upon his seed, much less to share in them. This is promised to Josiah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.20">2 Kings xxii. 20</reference>. Note, Good men are sometimes greatly favoured by being <hi type="italic">taken away from the evil to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa. lvii. 1</reference>. Let this satisfy Abram, that, for his part, <div eID="gen580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen581" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shall <hi type="italic">go to his fathers in peace.</hi> Note, [1.] Even the friends and favourites of Heaven are not exempted from the stroke of death. Are we greater than our father Abram, who is dead? <reference osisRef="John.8.53">John viii. 53</reference>. [2.] Good men die willingly; they are not fetched, they are not forced, but they go; their soul is not required, as the rich fool's (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 20</reference>), but cheerfully resigned: they would not live always. [3.] At death we go to our fathers, to all our fathers that have gone before us to the state of the dead (<reference osisRef="Job.21.32-Job.21.33">Job xxi. 32, 33</reference>), to our godly fathers that have gone before us to the state of the blessed, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">Heb. xii. 23</reference>. The former thought helps to take off the terror of death, the latter puts comfort into it. [4.] Whenever a godly man dies, he dies in peace. If the way be piety, the end is peace, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">Ps. xxxvii. 37</reference>. Outward peace, to the last, is promised to Abram, peace and truth is his days, whatever should come afterwards (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.19">2 Kings xx. 19</reference>); peace with God, and everlasting peace, are sure to all the seed. <div eID="gen581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen582" type="x-p"/> (2.) He shall be <hi type="italic">buried in a good old age.</hi> Perhaps mention is made of his burial here, where the land of Canaan is promised him, because a burying place was the first possession he had in it. He shall not only die in peace, but die in honour, die, and be buried decently; not only die in peace, but die in season, <reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job v. 26</reference>. Note, [1.] Old age is a blessing. It is promised in the fifth commandment; it is pleasing to nature; and it affords a great opportunity for usefulness. [2.] Especially, if it be a good old age. Theirs may be called a good old age, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That are old and healthful, not loaded with such distempers as make them weary of life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That are old and holy, old disciples (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.16">Acts xxi. 16</reference>), whose hoary head is <hi type="italic">found in the way of righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.31">Prov. xvi. 31</reference>), old and useful, old and exemplary for godliness; theirs is indeed a good old age.
entries.4c4ce8bf7a804ce6515de8a6072e165319e1c047: <div eID="gen582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen583" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And it came to pass, that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp that passed between those pieces. <hi type="super">18</hi> In the same day the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates: <hi type="super">19</hi> The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites, <hi type="super">20</hi> And the Hittites, and the Perizzites, and the Rephaims, <hi type="super">21</hi> And the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites. <div eID="gen583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen584" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The covenant ratified (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">v. 17</reference>); the sign which Abram desired was given, at length, when the sun had gone down, so that it was dark; for that was a dark dispensation. <div eID="gen584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen585" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">smoking furnace</hi> signified the affliction of his seed in Egypt. They were there in the <hi type="italic">iron furnace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">Deut. iv. 20</reference>), the <hi type="italic">furnace of affliction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa. xlviii. 10</reference>), labouring in the very fire. They were there in the smoke, their eyes darkened, that they could not see to the end of their troubles, and themselves at a loss to conceive what God would do with them. Clouds and darkness were round about them. <div eID="gen585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen586" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">burning lamp</hi> denotes comfort in this affliction; and this God showed to Abram, at the same time that he showed him the <hi type="italic">smoking furnace.</hi> (1.) Light denotes deliverance out of the furnace; their salvation was as <hi type="italic">a lamp that burneth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.62.1">Isa. lxii. 1</reference>. When God came down to deliver them, he appeared in a bush that <hi type="italic">burned, and was not consumed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.3.2">Exod. iii. 2</reference>. (2.) The lamp denotes direction in the smoke. God's word was their lamp: this word to Abram was so, it was a light shining in a dark place. Perhaps this burning lamp prefigured the pillar of cloud and fire, which led them out of Egypt, in which God was. (3.) The burning lamp denotes the destruction of their enemies who kept them so long in the furnace. See <reference osisRef="Zech.12.6">Zech. xii. 6</reference>. The same cloud that enlightened the Israelites troubled and burned the Egyptians. <div eID="gen586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen587" type="x-p"/> 3. The passing of these between the pieces was the confirming of the covenant God now made with him, that he might have strong consolation, being fully persuaded that what God promised he would certainly perform. It is probable that the furnace and lamp, which passed between the pieces, burnt and consumed them, and so completed the sacrifice, and testified God's acceptance of it, as of Gideon's (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.21">Judg. vi. 21</reference>), Manoah's (<reference osisRef="Judg.13.19-Judg.13.20">Judg. xiii. 19, 20</reference>), and Solomon's, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1">2 Chron. vii. 1</reference>. So it intimates, (1.) That God's covenants with man are made by sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.5">Ps. l. 5</reference>), by Christ, the great sacrifice: no agreement without atonement. (2.) God's acceptance of our spiritual sacrifices is a token for good and an earnest of further favours. See <reference osisRef="Judg.13.23">Judg. xiii. 23</reference>. And by this we may know that he accepts our sacrifices if he kindle in our souls a holy fire of pious and devout affections in them. <div eID="gen587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen588" type="x-p"/> II. The covenant repeated and explained: <hi type="italic">In that same day,</hi> that day never to be forgotten, <hi type="italic">the Lord made a covenant with Abram,</hi> that is, gave a promise to Abram, saying, <hi type="italic">Unto thy seed have I given this land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">v. 18</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen589" type="x-p"/> 1. A rehearsal of the grant. He had said before, <hi type="italic">To thy seed will I give this land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.12.7">ch. xii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.13.15">xiii. 15</reference>. But here he says, <hi type="italic">I have given it;</hi> that is, (1.) I have given the promise of it, the charter is sealed and delivered, and cannot be disannulled. Note, God's promises are God's gifts, and are so to be accounted. (2.) The possession is as sure, in due time, as if it were now actually delivered to them. What God has promised is as sure as if it were already done; hence, it is said, <hi type="italic">He that believes hath everlasting life</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>), for he shall as surely go to heaven as if he were there already. <div eID="gen589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen590" type="x-p"/> 2. A recital of the particulars granted, such as is usual in the grants of lands. He specifies the boundaries of the land intended hereby to be granted, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">v. 18</reference>. And then, for the greater certainty, as is usual in such cases, he mentions in whose tenure and occupation these lands now were. Ten several nations, or tribes, are here spoken of (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.19-Gen.15.21">v. 19-21</reference>) that must be cast out, to make room for the <hi type="italic">seed of Abram.</hi> They were not possessed of all these countries when God brought them into Canaan. The bounds are fixed much narrower, <reference osisRef="Num.34.2-Num.34.12">Num. xxxiv. 2, 3</reference>. &c. But, (1.) In David's time, and Solomon's, their jurisdiction extended to the utmost of these limits, <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.26">2 Chron. ix. 26</reference>. (2.) It was their own fault that they were not sooner and longer in possession of all these territories. They forfeited their right by their sins, and by their own sloth and cowardice kept themselves out of possession. (3.) The land granted is here described in its utmost extent because it was to be a type of the heavenly inheritance, where there is room enough: in our father's house are many mansions. The present occupants are named, because their number, and strength, and long prescription, should be no hindrance to the accomplishment of this promise in its season, and to magnify God's love to Abram and his seed, in giving to that one nation the possessions of many nations, so precious were they in his sight, and so honourable, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 4</reference>.  <chapter eID="Gen.15"/> <div eID="gen590" type="x-p"/>

entries.207de5b3935dc014cfbb7cab983300bc9fe71a11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv168"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.15.1-Gen.15.21">Ge 15:1-21</reference>. Divine Encouragement.</title> <div sID="gen325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv168"/><hi type="bold">1. After these things--</hi>the conquest of the invading kings.<div eID="gen325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the word of the Lord--</hi>a phrase used, when connected with a vision, to denote a prophetic message.<div eID="gen326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Fear not, Abram--</hi>When the excitement of the enterprise was over, he had become a prey to despondency and terror at the probable revenge that might be meditated against him. To dispel his fear, he was favored with this gracious announcement. Having such a promise, how well did it become him (and all God's people who have the same promise) to dismiss fears, and cast all burdens on the Lord (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.3">Psa 27:3</reference>). <div eID="gen327" type="x-p"/>
entries.699b9407e58a1d024e0ef76abb23b20e13ecc16a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv169"/><div sID="gen328" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv169"/><hi type="bold">2. Lord God, what wilt thou give?--</hi>To his mind the declaration, "I am thy exceeding great reward" [Ge 15:1], had but one meaning, or was viewed but in one particular light, as bearing on the fulfilment of the promise, and he was still experiencing the sickness of hope deferred. <div eID="gen328" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e018c82692ff7eea0bacc3953c58221072cd8e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv170"/><div sID="gen329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv170"/><hi type="bold">3. Eliezer of Damascus ... one born in my house is mine heir--</hi>According to the usage of nomadic tribes, his chief confidential servant, would be heir to his possessions and honors. But this man could have become his son only by adoption; and how sadly would that have come short of the parental hopes he had been encouraged to entertain! His language betrayed a latent spirit of fretfulness or perhaps a temporary failure in the very virtue for which he is so renowned--and absolute submission to God's time, as well as way, of accomplishing His promise. <div eID="gen329" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d32c87e8be41f63069b78ee05c710be8e749fda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv171"/><div sID="gen330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv171"/><hi type="bold">4. This shall not be thine heir--</hi>To the first part of his address no reply was given; but having renewed it in a spirit of more becoming submission, "whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it" [Ge 15:8], he was delighted by a most explicit promise of Canaan, which was immediately confirmed by a remarkable ceremony. <div eID="gen330" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d39d35a392c7dd9d8997f4b6d5a8762051f762e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv172"/><div sID="gen331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv172"/><hi type="bold">9-21. Take me an heifer, &c.--</hi>On occasions of great importance, when two or more parties join in a compact, they either observe precisely the same rites as Abram did, or, where they do not, they invoke the lamp as their witness. According to these ideas, which have been from time immemorial engraven on the minds of Eastern people, the Lord Himself condescended to enter into covenant with Abram. The patriarch did not pass between the sacrifice and the reason was that in this transaction he was bound to nothing. He asked a sign, and God was pleased to give him a sign, by which, according to Eastern ideas, He bound Himself. In like manner God has entered into covenant with us; and in the glory of the only-begotten Son, who passed through between God and us, all who believe have, like Abram, a sign or pledge in the gift of the Spirit, whereby they may know that they shall inherit the heavenly Canaan. <chapter eID="Gen.15"/>

entries.62d994aa9c902b9919643c905b64321cdae36beb: <div eID="gen702" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen703" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen704" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen704" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen703" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen705" type="x-p"/> God appears to Abram in a vision, and gives him great encouragement, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference>. Abram's request and complaint, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.2">Gen 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.3">Gen 15:3</reference>. God promises him a son, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.4">Gen 15:4</reference>; and an exceedingly numerous posterity, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Gen 15:5</reference>. Abram credits the promise, and his faith is counted unto him for righteousness, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">Gen 15:6</reference>. Jehovah proclaims himself, and renews the promise of Canaan to his posterity, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.7">Gen 15:7</reference>. Abram requires a sign of its fulfillment, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">Gen 15:8</reference>. Jehovah directs him to offer a sacrifice of five different animals, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9">Gen 15:9</reference>; which he accordingly does, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.10">Gen 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.11">Gen 15:11</reference>. God reveals to him the affliction of his posterity in Egypt, and the duration of that affliction, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.12">Gen 15:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.13">Gen 15:13</reference>. Promises to bring them back to the land of Canaan with great affluence, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.14-Gen.15.16">Gen 15:14-16</reference>. Renews the covenant with Abram, and mentions the possessions which should be given to his posterity, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18-Gen.15.21">Gen 15:18-21</reference>. <div eID="gen705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen706" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen707" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord came unto Abram - This is the first place where God is represented as revealing himself by his word. Some learned men suppose that the דבר יהוה debar Yehovah, translated here word of the Lord, means the same with the λογος του Θεου of St. John, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>, and, by the Chaldee paraphrases in the next clause, called מימרי meimeri, "my word," and in other places מימרא דיי meimera daiya, the word of Yeya, a contraction for Jehovah, which they appear always to consider as a person; and which they distinguish from פתגמא pithgama, which signifies merely a word spoken, or any part of speech. There have been various conjectures concerning the manner in which God revealed his will, not only to the patriarchs, but also to the prophets, evangelists, and apostles. It seems to have been done in different ways. 1. By a personal appearance of him who was afterwards incarnated for the salvation of mankind. 2. By an audible voice, sometimes accompanied with emblematical appearances. 3. By visions which took place either in the night in ordinary sleep, or when the persons were cast into a temporary trance by daylight, or when about their ordinary business, 4. By the ministry of angels appearing in human bodies, and performing certain miracles to accredit their mission. 5. By the powerful agency of the Spirit of God upon the mind, giving it a strong conception and supernatural persuasion of the truth of the things perceived by the understanding. We shall see all these exemplified in the course of the work. It was probably in the third sense that the revelation in the text was given; for it is said, God appeared to Abram in a vision, מחזה machazeh, from חזה chazah, to see, or according to others, to fix, fasten, settle; hence chozeh, a Seer, the person who sees Divine things, to whom alone they are revealed, on whose mind they are fastened, and in whose memory and judgment they are fixed and settled. Hence the vision which was mentally perceived, and, by the evidence to the soul of its Divine origin, fixed and settled in the mind. <div eID="gen707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen708" type="x-p"/> Fear not - The late Dr. Dodd has a good thought on this passage; "I would read, says he, "the second verse in a parenthesis, thus: For Abram Had said, Lord God, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, etc. Abram had said this in the fear of his heart, upon which the Lord vouchsafed to him this prophetical view, and this strong renovation of the covenant. In this light all follows very properly. Abram had said so and so in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.2">Gen 15:2</reference>, upon which God appears and says, I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward. The patriarch then, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.3">Gen 15:3</reference>, freely opens the anxious apprehension of his heart, Behold, to me thou hast given no seed, etc., upon which God proceeds to assure him of posterity." <div eID="gen708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen709" type="x-p"/> I am thy shield, etc. - Can it be supposed that Abram understood these words as promising him temporal advantages at all corresponding to the magnificence of these promises? If he did he was disappointed through the whole course of his life, for he never enjoyed such a state of worldly prosperity as could justify the strong language in the text. Shall we lose sight of Abram, and say that his posterity was intended, and Abram understood the promises as relating to them, and not to himself or immediately to his own family? Then the question recurs, Did the Israelites ever enjoy such a state of temporal affluence as seems to be intended by the above promise? To this every man acquainted with their history will, without hesitation, say, No. What then is intended? Just what the words state. God was Abram's portion, and he is the portion of every righteous soul; for to Abram, and the children of his faith, he gives not a portion in this life. Nothing, says Father Calmet, proves more invincibly the immortality of the soul, the truth of religion, and the eternity of another life, than to see that in this life the righteous seldom receive the reward of their virtue, and that in temporal things they are often less happy than the workers of iniquity. <div eID="gen709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen710" type="x-p"/> I am, says the Almighty, thy shield - thy constant covering and protector, and thy exceeding great reward, שכרך הרבה מאד sekarcha harbeh meod, "That superlatively multiplied reward of thine." It is not the Canaan I promise, but the salvation that is to come through the promised seed. Hence it was that Abram rejoiced to see his day. And hence the Chaldee Targum translates this place, My Word shall be thy strength, etc.
entries.b1a27a1aec7048251da1cba520c6089511381001: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen711" type="x-p"/> What wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless - The anxiety of the Asiatics to have offspring is intense and universal. Among the Hindoos the want of children renders all other blessings of no esteem. See Ward. <div eID="gen711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen712" type="x-p"/> And the steward of my house - Abram, understanding the promise as relating to that person who was to spring from his family, in whom all the nations of the earth should be blessed, expresses his surprise that there should be such a promise, and yet he is about to die childless! How then can the promise be fulfilled, when, far from a spiritual seed, he has not even a person in his family that has a natural right to his property, and that a stranger is likely to be his heir? This seems to be the general sense of the passage; but who this steward of his house, this Eliezer of Damascus, was, commentators are not agreed. The translation of the Septuagint is at least curious: Ὁδε υἱος Μασεκ της οικολενους μου, οὑτος Δαμασκος Ελιεζερ·. The son of Masek my homeborn maid, this Eliezer of Damascus, is my heir; which intimates that they supposed משק meshek, which we translate steward, to have been the name of a female slave, born in the family of Abram, of whom was born this Eliezer, who on account of the country either of his father or mother, was called a Damascene or one of Damascus. It is extremely probable that our Lord has this passage in view in his parable of the rich man and Lazarus, <reference osisRef="Luk.16.19">Luk 16:19</reference>. From the name Eliezer, by leaving out the first letter, Liezer is formed, which makes Lazarus in the New Testament, the person who, from an abject and distressed state, was raised to lie in the bosom of Abraham in paradise.
entries.75fa219f8634cad65e7b83c3c9d382123cac8d5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen713" type="x-p"/> Look now toward heaven - It appears that this whole transaction took place in the evening; see on <reference osisRef="Gen.13.14">Gen 13:14</reference> (note). Abram had either two visions, that recorded in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference>, and that in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.12">Gen 15:12</reference>, etc.; or what is mentioned in the beginning of this chapter is a part of the occurrences which took place after the sacrifice mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9">Gen 15:9</reference>, etc.: but it is more likely that there was a vision of that kind already described, and afterwards a second, in which he received the revelation mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.15.13-Gen.15.16">Gen 15:13-16</reference>. After the first vision he is brought forth abroad to see if he can number the stars; and as he finds this impossible, he is assured that as they are to him innumerable, so shall his posterity be; and that all should spring from one who should proceed from his own bowels - one who should be his own legitimate child.
entries.bcafc015a3d8ed1dd6ea7b972f48a1dc420d195b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen714" type="x-p"/> And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness - This I conceive to be one of the most important passages in the whole Old Testament. It properly contains and specifies that doctrine of justification by faith which engrosses so considerable a share of the epistles of St. Paul, and at the foundation of which is the atonement made by the Son of God: And he (Abram) believed האמן heemin, he put faith) in Jehovah, ויחשבה לו vaiyachshebeita lo, and he counted it - the faith he put in Jehovah, to Him for righteousness, צדקה tsedakah, or justification; though there was no act in the case but that of the mind and heart, no work of any kind. Hence the doctrine of justification by faith, without any merit of works; for in this case there could be none - no works of Abram which could merit the salvation of the whole human race. It was the promise of God which he credited, and in the blessedness of which he became a partaker through faith. See at <reference osisRef="Gen.15.19">Gen 15:19</reference> (note); see also on Romans 4 (note).
entries.ffa446b6fc63ebb90830356a2d997ef20218b7f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen715" type="x-p"/> Ur of the Chaldees - See on Genesis 40 (note).
entries.bc4ffb7aa09a2f2f6f7a1d0dd467a3c1dfafeae1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen716" type="x-p"/> And he said, Lord God - אדני יהוה Adonai Yehovah, my Lord Jehovah. Adonai is the word which the Jews in reading always substitute for Jehovah, as they count it impious to pronounce this name. Adonai signifies my director, basis, supporter, prop, or stay; and scarcely a more appropriate name can be given to that God who is the framer and director of every righteous word and action; the basis or foundation on which every rational hope rests; the supporter of the souls and bodies of men, as well as of the universe in general; the prop and stay of the weak and fainting, and the buttress that shores up the building, which otherwise must necessarily fall. This word often occurs in the Hebrew Bible, and is rendered in our translation Lord; the same term by which the word Jehovah is expressed: but to distinguish between the two, and to show the reader when the original is יהוה Yehovah, and when אדני Adonai, the first is always put in capitals, Lord, the latter in plain Roman characters, Lord. For the word Jehovah see on <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen 2:4</reference> (note), and on <reference osisRef="Exo.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference> (note). <div eID="gen716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen717" type="x-p"/> Whereby shall I know - By what sign shall I be assured, that I shall inherit this land? It appears that he expected some sign, and that on such occasions one was ordinarily given.
entries.aee7656616d2af2bb675ba82ee92adc5a9d2dab8: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen718" type="x-p"/> Take me a heifer - עגלה eglah, a she-calf; a she-goat, עז ez, a goat, male or female, but distinguished here by the feminine adjective; משלשת meshullesheth, a three-yearling; a ram, איל ayil; a turtle-dove, תר tor, from which come turtur and turtle; young pigeon, גוזל gozal, a word signifying the young of pigeons and eagles. See <reference osisRef="Deu.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference>. It is worthy of remark, that every animal allowed or commanded to be sacrificed under the Mosaic law is to be found in this list. And is it not a proof that God was now giving to Abram an epitome of that law and its sacrifices which he intended more fully to reveal to Moses; the essence of which consisted in its sacrifices, which typified the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world? <div eID="gen718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen719" type="x-p"/> On the several animals which God ordered Abram to take, Jarchi remarks: "The idolatrous nations are compared in the Scriptures to bulls, rams, and goats; for it is written, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.12">Psa 22:12</reference> : Many bulls have compassed me about. <reference osisRef="Dan.8.20">Dan 8:20</reference> : The ram which thou hast seen is the king of Persia. The rough goat is the king of Greece. <reference osisRef="Dan.8.21">Dan 8:21</reference>. But the Israelites are compared to doves, etc.; <reference osisRef="Sol.2.14">Sol 2:14</reference> : "O my dove, that art in the cleft of the rock. The division of the above carcasses denotes the division and extermination of the idolatrous nations; but the birds not being divided, shows that the Israelites are to abide for ever." See Jarchi on the place.
entries.65846d2e4765e533ed1fa2f79af8483a0c4d9832: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen720" type="x-p"/> Divided them in the midst - The ancient method of making covenants as well as the original word, have been already alluded to, and in a general way explained. See <reference osisRef="Gen.6.18">Gen 6:18</reference>. The word covenant from con, together, and venio, I come, signifies an agreement, association, or meeting between two or more parties; for it is impossible that a covenant can be made between an individual and himself, whether God or man. This is a theological absurdity into which many have run; there must be at least two parties to contract with each other. And often there was a third party to mediate the agreement, and to witness it when made. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi says, "It was a custom with those who entered into covenant with each other to take a heifer and cut it in two, and then the contracting parties passed between the pieces." See this and the scriptures to which it refers particularly explained, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.18">Gen 6:18</reference>. A covenant always supposed one of these four things: <div eID="gen720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen721" type="x-p"/> 1. That the contracting parties had been hitherto unknown to each other, and were brought by the covenant into a state of acquaintance. <div eID="gen721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen722" type="x-p"/> 2. That they had been previously in a state of hostility or enmity, and were brought by the covenant into a state of pacification and friendship. <div eID="gen722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen723" type="x-p"/> 3. Or that, being known to each other, they now agree to unite their counsels, strength, property, etc., for the accomplishment of a particular purpose, mutually subservient to the interests of both. Or, <div eID="gen723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen724" type="x-p"/> 4. It implies an agreement to succor and defend a third party in cases of oppression and distress. <div eID="gen724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen725" type="x-p"/> For whatever purpose a covenant was made, it was ever ratified by a sacrifice offered to God; and the passing between the divided parts of the victim appears to have signified that each agreed, if they broke their engagements, to submit to the punishment of being cut asunder; which we find from <reference osisRef="Mat.24.51">Mat 24:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.12.46">Luk 12:46</reference>, was an ancient mode of punishment. This is farther confirmed by Herodotus, who says that Sabacus, king of Ethiopia, had a vision, in which he was ordered μεσους διατεμειν, to cut in two, all the Egyptian priests; lib. ii. We find also from the same author, lib. vii., that Xerxes ordered one of the sons of Pythius μεσον διατεμειν, to be cut in two, and one half to be placed on each side of the way, that his army might pass through between them. That this kind of punishment was used among the Persians we have proof from <reference osisRef="Dan.2.5">Dan 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.3.29">Dan 3:29</reference>. Story of Susanna, verses 55, 59. See farther, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sam 12:31</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">1Chr 20:3</reference>. These authorities may be sufficient to show that the passing between the parts of the divided victims signified the punishment to which those exposed themselves who broke their covenant engagements. And that covenant sacrifices were thus divided, even from the remotest antiquity, we learn from Homer, Il. A., v. 460. Μηρους τ' εξεταμον κατα τε κνισοῃ εκαλυψαν, Διπτυχα ποιησαντες, επ' αυτων δ' ωμοθετησαν. "They cut the quarters, and cover them with the fat; dividing them into two, they place the raw flesh upon them." <div eID="gen725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen726" type="x-p"/> But this place may be differently understood. <div eID="gen726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen727" type="x-p"/> St. Cyril, in his work against Julian, shows that passing between the divided parts of a victim was used also among the Chaldeans and other people. As the sacrifice was required to make an atonement to God, so the death of the animal was necessary to signify to the contracting parties the punishment to which they exposed themselves, should they prove unfaithful. <div eID="gen727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen728" type="x-p"/> Livy preserves the form of the imprecation used on such occasions, in the account he gives of the league made between the Romans and Albans. When the Romans were about to enter into some solemn league or covenant, they sacrificed a hog; and, on the above occasion, the priest, or pater patratus, before he slew the animal, stood, and thus invoked Jupiter: <div eID="gen728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen729" type="x-p"/> Audi, Jupiter! Si prior defecerit publico consilio dolo malo, tum illo die, Diespiter, Populum Romanum sic ferito, ut ego hune porcum hic hodie feriam; tantoque magis ferito, quanto magis potes pollesque! - Livii Hist., lib. i., chap. 24. "Hear, O Jupiter! Should the Romans in public counsel, through any evil device, first transgress these laws, in that same day, O Jupiter, thus smite the Roman people, as I shall at this time smite this hog; and smite them with a severity proportioned to the greatness of thy power and might!" <div eID="gen729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen730" type="x-p"/> But the birds divided he not - According to the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.17">Lev 1:17</reference>, fowls were not to be divided asunder but only cloven for the purpose of taking out the intestines.
entries.881cec8ecd5e67256c2b36806e7359f19460f8db: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen731" type="x-p"/> And when the fowls - העיט haayit, birds of prey, came down upon the carcasses to devour them, Abram, who stood by his sacrifice waiting for the manifestation of God, who had ordered him to prepare for the ratification of the covenant, drove them away, that they might neither pollute nor devour what had been thus consecrated to God.
entries.01fdaa2e702ddd3c929753466fe48fcc6daccabb: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen732" type="x-p"/> A deep sleep - תרדמה tardemah, the same word which is used to express the sleep into which Adam was cast, previous to the formation of Eve; <reference osisRef="Gen.2.21">Gen 2:21</reference>. <div eID="gen732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen733" type="x-p"/> A horror of great darkness - Which God designed to be expressive of the affliction and misery into which his posterity should be brought during the four hundred years of their bondage in Egypt; as the next verse particularly states.
entries.b36f54375439fedf0112a12bfefd088b3ee50ce4: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen734" type="x-p"/> Four hundred years - "Which began," says Mr. Ainsworth, "when Ishmael, son of Hagar, mocked and persecuted Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.9">Gen 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.29">Gal 4:29</reference>; which fell out thirty years after the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen 12:3</reference>; which promise was four hundred and thirty years before the law, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.17">Gal 3:17</reference>; and four hundred and thirty years after that promise came Israel out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exo.12.41">Exo 12:41</reference>."
entries.99ede8c53ea22a195ea3d4a9d7e761caba17f805: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen735" type="x-p"/> And also that nation, etc. - How remarkably was this promise fulfilled, in the redemption of Israel from its bondage, in the plagues and destruction of the Egyptians, and in the immense wealth which the Israelites brought out of Egypt! Not a more circumstantial or literally fulfilled promise is to be found in the sacred writings.
entries.07409e4a53f4e7bf1254c6be97274760d2d242b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen736" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace - This verse strongly implies the immortality of the soul, and a state of separate existence. He was gathered to his fathers - introduced into the place where separate spirits are kept, waiting for the general resurrection. Two things seem to be distinctly marked here: <div eID="gen736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen737" type="x-p"/> 1. The soul of Abram should be introduced among the assembly of the first-born; Thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace. <div eID="gen737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen738" type="x-p"/> 2. His body should be buried after a long life, one hundred and seventy-five years, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.7">Gen 25:7</reference>. The body was buried; the soul went to the spiritual world, to dwell among the fathers - the patriarchs, who had lived and died in the Lord. See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.25.8">Gen 25:8</reference>.
entries.7c4f60f3240dc2cfb9d79bf9db1f1bbd3ed9c1cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen739" type="x-p"/> In the fourth generation - In former times most people counted by generations, to each of which was assigned a term of years amounting to 20, 25, 30, 33, 100, 108, or 110; for the generation was of various lengths among various people, at different times. It is probable that the fourth generation here means the same as the four hundred years in the preceding verse. Some think it refers to the time when Eleazar, the son of Aaron, the son of Amram, the son of Kohath, came out of Egypt, and divided the land of Canaan to Israel, <reference osisRef="Jos.14.1">Jos 14:1</reference>. Others think the fourth generation of the Amorites is intended, because it is immediately added, The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full; but in the fourth generation they should be expelled, and the descendants of Abram established in their place. From these words we learn that there is a certain pitch of iniquity to which nations may arrive before they are destroyed, and beyond which Divine justice does not permit them to pass.
entries.75bb3339ab1d60e78a59a0ec226489631b41b971: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen740" type="x-p"/> Smoking furnace and a burning lamp - Probably the smoking furnace might be designed as an emblem of the sore afflictions of the Israelites in Egypt; but the burning lamp was certainly the symbol of the Divine presence, which, passing between the pieces, ratified the covenant with Abram, as the following verse immediately states.
entries.b95de073af1c7697196df38c6000c682e70b4354: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen741" type="x-p"/> The Lord made a covenant - כרת ברית carath berith signifies to cut a covenant, or rather the covenant sacrifice; for as no covenant was made without one, and the creature was cut in two that the contracting parties might pass between the pieces, hence cutting the covenant signified making the covenant. The same form of speech obtained among the Romans; and because, in making their covenants they always slew an animal, either by cutting its throat, or knocking it down with a stone or axe, after which they divided the parts as we have already seen, hence among the percutere faedus, to smite a covenant, and scindere faedus, to cleave a covenant, were terms which signified simply to make or enter into a covenant. <div eID="gen741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen742" type="x-p"/> From the river of Egypt - Not the Nile, but the river called Sichor, which was before or on the border of Egypt, near to the isthmus of Suez; see <reference osisRef="Jos.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>; though some think that by this a branch of the Nile is meant. This promise was fully accomplished in the days of David and Solomon. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sam 8:3</reference>, etc., and <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.26">2Chr 9:26</reference>.
entries.85bf225ae94b5d0033711de417e9af2fe90c43b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen743" type="x-p"/> The Kenites, etc. - Here are ten nations mentioned, though afterwards reckoned but seven; see <reference osisRef="Deu.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.13.19">Act 13:19</reference>. Probably some of them which existed in Abram's time had been blended with others before the time of Moses, so that seven only out of the ten then remained; see part of these noticed Genesis 10. <div eID="gen743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen744" type="x-p"/> In this chapter there are three subjects which must be particularly interesting to the pious reader. 1. The condescension of God in revealing himself to mankind in a variety of ways, so as to render it absolutely evident that he had spoken, that he loved mankind, and that he had made every provision for their eternal welfare. So unequivocal were the discoveries which God made of himself, that on the minds of those to whom they were made not one doubt was left, relative either to the truth of the subject, or that it was God himself who made the discovery.
